```{r setup-results, include = FALSE}
# Every number in this section is read from output/tables/*.csv, which are written by
# analysis.R (steps/00-10). Nothing is estimated here; this file only formats results.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(kableExtra)
library(knitr)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

tab <- function(x) readr::read_csv(here::here("output", "tables", paste0(x, ".csv")), show_col_types = FALSE)
fig <- function(x) here::here("output", "figures", x)

# ---- formatting helpers ----------------------------------------------------------
num <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", ifelse(p < 0.01, sprintf("p = %.3f", p), sprintf("p = %.2f", p)))
ci <- function(r, scale = 1, d = 2) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", num(r$est * scale, d), num(r$lo * scale, d), num(r$hi * scale, d))
one <- function(df, ...) {
  out <- dplyr::filter(df, ...)
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1)
  out
}

# ---- results read from the analysis pipeline ---------------------------------------
raw <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/data/processed/tutorgpt.rds")) %>% filter(student_id > 1)
chats <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/data/processed/chats.rds")) %>% filter(user_id != 1)

sample_arm <- tab("sample_by_school_arm")
smd <- tab("balance_smd")
bal_joint <- tab("balance_joint_test")
ss <- tab("summary_statistics")

rs_desc <- tab("reasoning_descriptives")
rs_eff <- tab("reasoning_effects")
pa_desc <- tab("perceived_accuracy_descriptives")
pa_eff <- tab("perceived_accuracy_effects")

conf_desc <- tab("confidence_descriptives")
conf_eff <- tab("confidence_effects")
conf_size <- tab("confidence_effect_sizes")
conf_pool <- tab("confidence_pooled")
corr_desc <- tab("correctness_descriptives")
corr_eff <- tab("correctness_effects")
corr_or <- tab("correctness_odds_ratio")
trans <- tab("learning_transitions")
calib <- tab("calibration_means")
calib_int <- tab("calibration_interaction")
retention <- tab("retention_effects")
holm <- tab("primary_holm")
ri <- tab("primary_randomisation_inference")
robust <- tab("primary_robustness")
mde <- tab("primary_mde")
het <- tab("exploratory_heterogeneity_school")

help_desc <- tab("helpfulness_descriptives")
help_eff <- tab("helpfulness_effects")
help_chk <- tab("helpfulness_checks")
help_pool <- tab("helpfulness_pooled")

vol <- tab("tab_llm_volume_tests")
vol_desc <- tab("tab_llm_interaction_volume")
use <- tab("exploratory_tutor_usage")
rel <- tab("tab_llm_reliability")
llm <- tab("tab_llm_effects")
llm_rater <- tab("tab_llm_per_rater")
llm_sens <- tab("tab_llm_sensitivity")
llm_r2 <- tab("tab_llm_length_r2")
op_desc <- tab("exploratory_opinion_descriptives")
op_eff <- tab("exploratory_opinion_effects")

# ---- derived quantities used in the text -----------------------------------------------
n_all <- nrow(raw)
n_bru <- sum(raw$location == "Brussels")
n_sev <- sum(raw$location == "Seville")
n_an <- sum(sample_arm$n)                                    # analysis sample (complete on the primary outcomes)
n_soc <- sum(sample_arm$n[sample_arm$arm == "Socratic"])
n_non <- sum(sample_arm$n[sample_arm$arm == "Non-Socratic"])

p_fisher <- ss %>% distinct(name, pval, pval_explain)
n_tests <- 2 * nrow(p_fisher)
n_sig <- sum(p_fisher$pval < 0.05) + sum(p_fisher$pval_explain < 0.05)
p_min_fisher <- min(c(p_fisher$pval, p_fisher$pval_explain))

agree <- function(v) 100 * mean(raw[[v]] %in% c("agree", "strongly_agree"), na.rm = TRUE)
easy <- function(v) 100 * mean(raw[[v]] == "Could do easily", na.rm = TRUE)

# Conversation logs: accounts and accounts seen under both conditions
acct <- chats %>% distinct(chat_id, user_id, treatment_tutor_id) %>% group_by(user_id) %>% summarise(arms = n_distinct(treatment_tutor_id))
n_accounts <- nrow(acct)
n_both <- sum(acct$arms > 1)

# Task 3 correctness pooled over arms
pct_before <- sum(corr_desc$pct_correct_before * corr_desc$n) / sum(corr_desc$n)
pct_after <- sum(corr_desc$pct_correct_after * corr_desc$n) / sum(corr_desc$n)
tr_rate <- function(a, pre, post) trans %>% filter(arm == a, pre_correct == pre, post_correct == post) %>% pull(pct_of_row)

task_name <- c(C1 = "Task 1: water estimate", C2 = "Task 2: social-media essay", C3 = "Task 3: sound physics")
c_ols <- function(id) one(conf_eff, outcome == id, model == "OLS, adjusted (points)")
r_rs <- function(o, s = "adjusted") one(rs_eff, spec == s, outcome == o)
h_ols <- function(k) one(help_eff, grepl(k, task), model == "OLS, adjusted (points)")
h_or <- function(k) one(help_eff, grepl(k, task), model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)")
rs_m <- function(m, arm) rs_desc[[arm]][rs_desc$measure == m]
conduct_items <- c("supportive_guidance", "next_step_guidance", "encouraging_tone", "conversational_flow")
rel_c <- filter(rel, rubric == "socratic", mode == "full", item %in% conduct_items)
```

# Results {#sec:results}

We first describe the sample and the randomisation (Section \@ref(sec:res-sample)). We then report the first experiment, on AI-generated explanations (RQ1 and RQ2), and the second, on Socratic versus non-Socratic AI agents (RQ3 to RQ5). In the second experiment the four primary outcomes are the students' confidence in their answer in each of the three tasks and the correctness of the Task 3 answer; they are tested with a Holm correction across the four outcomes. Perceived helpfulness (RQ4), the analysis of the conversations (RQ5) and the heterogeneity analyses are reported with their own caveats and are not corrected jointly with the primary outcomes. All estimates come from the scripts in the `steps/` folder of the replication package.

## Sample and Randomisation {#sec:res-sample}

A total of `r n_all` students took part (`r n_bru` in Brussels and `r n_sev` in Seville), after excluding one test account. Primary outcomes are missing for `r n_all - n_an` of them, so the analyses of the second experiment use `r n_an` students (`r n_soc` with the Socratic and `r n_non` with the non-Socratic agent). The analyses of the first experiment use all `r n_all` students. Randomisation produced comparable groups (Table \@ref(tab:summary-statistics)). Of the `r n_tests` Fisher's exact tests of association between a characteristic and the assignment, `r ifelse(n_sig == 0, "none", n_sig)` reach`r ifelse(n_sig == 1, "es", "")` the 5% level, which is consistent with chance (the smallest p-value is `r num(p_min_fisher, 3)`, for self-reported difficulties with homework in the Socratic comparison). The standardised mean differences between the Socratic and non-Socratic groups are all below 0.25 in absolute value (the largest is `r num(max(abs(smd$smd)), 2)`; Figure \@ref(fig:balance)), and a joint test of whether the covariates predict assignment does not reject (likelihood-ratio $\chi^2$(`r bal_joint$df`) = `r num(bal_joint$chi2, 2)`, `r pv(bal_joint$p)`).

```{r summary-statistics}
ss %>%
  mutate(
    name = ifelse(row_number() == 1, name, ""),
    pval = ifelse(row_number() == 1, sprintf("%0.2f", pval), ""),
    pval_explain = ifelse(row_number() == 1, sprintf("%0.2f", pval_explain), ""),
    .by = name
  ) %>%
  select(name, value, percent_socratic, percent_non_socratic, pval,
         percent_explain_yes, percent_explain_no, pval_explain, totals) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(
    col.names = c("Name", "Value", "Yes", "No", "p", "Yes", "No", "p", "N"),
    digits = 0,
    booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = "Sample characteristics by treatment arm (percent of students in each arm). p is the p-value of a Fisher's exact test of association with the assignment.",
    linesep = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "\\hline" else ""
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) %>%
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Socratic AI (%)" = 3, "AI explanation (%)" = 3, " "))
```

```{r balance, fig.cap = "Standardised mean differences (Socratic minus non-Socratic) in baseline characteristics. The grey band marks |SMD| < 0.25.", out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("balance.pdf"))
```

The sample was balanced by gender (`r pct(100 * mean(raw$gender == "Girl", na.rm = TRUE))` girls) and `r pct(100 * mean(raw$has_used_before == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE))` of the students had used ChatGPT before. Students were not confident about the tasks on their own: only `r pct(easy("q5_self_physics"))` felt they could easily explain how sound propagates (Task 3) and `r pct(easy("q7_self_swimming_pool"))` that they could easily estimate a quantity such as the water consumed at school (Task 1), against `r pct(easy("q6_self_technology"))` for writing the essay (Task 2). Students held mixed views on AI in education (Figure \@ref(fig:attitudes-AI)): `r pct(agree("q4_ai_misuse"))` agreed that students often misuse AI and `r pct(agree("q2_ai_danger"))` that AI is dangerous, while `r pct(agree("q3_ai_learning"))` expected AI to foster students' learning and `r pct(agree("q1_ai_future"))` that society will benefit from it.

```{r attitudes-AI, fig.cap = "Student attitudes on AI in education", out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("fig_attitudes_AI.pdf"))
```

## Experiment 1: AI-Generated Explanations {#sec:res-explain}

All `r n_all` students first guessed the value of the coins in a jar, then saw the same AI estimate (US$ 213; the true value is US$ 379.54), and then revised their guess. Of them, `r rs_desc %>% filter(measure == "N") %>% pull(Explanation)` also saw the AI's step-by-step explanation.

### Estimation performance (RQ1) {#sec:res-rq1}

Nearly all students revised their guess after seeing the AI estimate, with no difference between the arms (`r pct(rs_m("Revised guess (%)", "No explanation"), 1)` without and `r pct(rs_m("Revised guess (%)", "Explanation"), 1)` with the explanation; Table \@ref(tab:reasoning)). Both groups also became much more accurate: the median absolute log error (in hundredths of a log point) fell from `r num(rs_m("Initial abs. log error (median)", "No explanation"), 0)` to `r num(rs_m("Final abs. log error (median)", "No explanation"), 0)` without the explanation and from `r num(rs_m("Initial abs. log error (median)", "Explanation"), 0)` to `r num(rs_m("Final abs. log error (median)", "Explanation"), 0)` with it (Figure \@ref(fig:reasoning-ecdf)). We do not test this before-after improvement, because the AI estimate was given to everyone; the question for RQ1 is whether the explanation changed what students did with it.

```{r reasoning}
groups <- rle(rs_desc$group)
ends <- cumsum(groups$lengths)
starts <- ends - groups$lengths + 1
tbl <- rs_desc %>%
  mutate(across(c("No explanation", "Explanation"), ~ ifelse(measure == "N", sprintf("%.0f", .x), sprintf("%.1f", .x)))) %>%
  select(measure, `No explanation`, Explanation) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(
    booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "c", "c"), col.names = c("Measure", "No explanation", "Explanation"),
    caption = "Descriptive statistics by explanation arm", linesep = ""
  )
for (i in seq_along(groups$values)) tbl <- kableExtra::pack_rows(tbl, groups$values[i], starts[i], ends[i], bold = TRUE)
tbl %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling() %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(
    general = "Absolute log errors are multiplied by 100. Within 10% means within 10% of the AI estimate in multiplicative terms. Guesses are in US dollars.",
    general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE
  )
```

```{r reasoning-ecdf, fig.cap = "Cumulative distribution of students' guesses of the value of the coins before and after seeing the AI estimate (USD 213), by explanation arm. Dotted lines mark the AI estimate and the true value (USD 379.54).", out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig(if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "fig_reasoning_ecdf.pdf" else "fig_reasoning_ecdf.png"))
```

```{r reasoning-eff}
lab <- c(adopt = "Adopted the AI estimate exactly (prob.)",
         near = "Final guess within 10% of the AI estimate (prob.)",
         err_final = "Final absolute log error (x 100)")
fmt_eff <- function(e, l, h, o) {
  s <- ifelse(o == "err_final", 100, 1)
  d <- ifelse(o == "err_final", 1, 2)
  mapply(function(e, l, h, s, d) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", num(e * s, d), num(l * s, d), num(h * s, d)), e, l, h, s, d)
}
rs_eff %>%
  mutate(outcome_lab = lab[outcome], effect = fmt_eff(est, lo, hi, outcome), p = sprintf("%.3f", p)) %>%
  select(outcome_lab, spec, effect, p, n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = spec, values_from = c(effect, p, n)) %>%
  select(outcome_lab, effect_unadjusted, p_unadjusted, n_unadjusted, effect_adjusted, p_adjusted, n_adjusted) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(
    booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "",
    col.names = c("Outcome", "Effect [95% CI]", "p", "N", "Effect [95% CI]", "p", "N"),
    caption = "Effect of seeing the AI's explanation (difference between arms; linear models with HC3 robust errors)"
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Unadjusted" = 3, "Adjusted" = 3)) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(
    general = "Adjusted models control for school, the initial guess, gender, grades and prior use of ChatGPT; students with missing gender or grades are dropped from them.",
    general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE
  )
```

Students who saw the explanation followed the AI estimate less closely. Only `r pct(rs_m("Adopted advice exactly (%)", "Explanation"), 1)` adopted it exactly, against `r pct(rs_m("Adopted advice exactly (%)", "No explanation"), 1)` of those who saw the estimate alone, and `r pct(rs_m("Final within 10% of advice (%)", "Explanation"), 1)` ended within 10% of it, against `r pct(rs_m("Final within 10% of advice (%)", "No explanation"), 1)`. In the adjusted model (Table \@ref(tab:reasoning-eff)) the explanation lowered the probability of ending within 10% of the estimate by `r num(-100 * r_rs("near")$est, 1)` percentage points (95% CI `r num(-100 * r_rs("near")$hi, 1)` to `r num(-100 * r_rs("near")$lo, 1)`; `r pv(r_rs("near")$p)`). The reduction in exact adoption is similar in size but less precisely estimated (`r num(-100 * r_rs("adopt")$est, 1)` points; `r pv(r_rs("adopt")$p)`).

However, we find no evidence that the explanation made the final guesses more accurate. The mean absolute log error differs by `r num(100 * r_rs("err_final")$est, 1)` points between the arms (95% CI `r num(100 * r_rs("err_final")$lo, 1)` to `r num(100 * r_rs("err_final")$hi, 1)`; `r pv(r_rs("err_final")$p)`), which rules out neither a modest benefit nor a modest harm. The lower median error in the explanation arm in Table \@ref(tab:reasoning) (`r num(rs_m("Final abs. log error (median)", "Explanation"), 1)` against `r num(rs_m("Final abs. log error (median)", "No explanation"), 1)`) is therefore not a reliable difference.^[`r ifelse(params$anonymous, "An earlier version of this manuscript", "An earlier working paper (SSRN, November 2025; https://ssrn.com/abstract=5040921)")` reported a significant reduction in the median absolute error in dollars, based on a one-sided bootstrap interval whose lower bound was zero, after removing one extreme guess. We do not retain that claim: it is not robust to keeping the extreme guess, and the analysis on the log scale reported here, which is not dominated by single extreme guesses, shows no difference.] We keep the one student who entered a guess of 6,969, since the log scale limits the influence of such a value.

### Perceived accuracy of the AI and of the human benchmark (RQ2) {#sec:res-rq2}

Students rated how accurate they thought the AI estimate was on a five-point scale. Without the explanation `r pct(one(pa_desc, target == "AI estimate", explain == "No")$pct_good)` of the students rated it good or very good, against `r pct(one(pa_desc, target == "AI estimate", explain == "Yes")$pct_good)` with the explanation (Table \@ref(tab:perceived)). The difference is not distinguishable from zero (ordinal-logit odds ratio `r ci(one(pa_eff, target == "AI estimate", model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)"))`, `r pv(one(pa_eff, target == "AI estimate", model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)")$p)`; Wilcoxon `r pv(one(pa_desc, target == "AI estimate", explain == "No")$wilcoxon_p)`). We therefore find no evidence that seeing the AI's reasoning changed the trust that students placed in its estimate.

```{r perceived}
fmt_row <- function(tg) {
  a <- one(pa_desc, target == tg, explain == "No")
  b <- one(pa_desc, target == tg, explain == "Yes")
  o <- one(pa_eff, target == tg, model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)")
  tibble(Target = tg,
         `Poor / very poor (No / Yes)` = sprintf("%.0f%% / %.0f%%", a$pct_poor, b$pct_poor),
         `Good / very good (No / Yes)` = sprintf("%.0f%% / %.0f%%", a$pct_good, b$pct_good),
         `Wilcoxon p` = sprintf("%.2f", a$wilcoxon_p), `Odds ratio [95% CI]` = ci(o), p = sprintf("%.3f", o$p))
}
bind_rows(fmt_row("AI estimate"), fmt_row("Human average")) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", caption = "Perceived accuracy of the two estimates, by whether students saw the AI's explanation (No / Yes)") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(
    general = "Odds ratios above 1 mean a higher perceived accuracy with the explanation; they come from ordinal logit models controlling for school, gender and prior use of ChatGPT (N = 120).",
    general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE
  )
```

The ratings of the human benchmark, the average guess of 600 people in the original study (US$ 596), tell a different story.^[The human average overestimated the true value by `r pct(100 * (596 / 379.54 - 1))`, while the AI estimate underestimated it by `r pct(100 * (1 - 213 / 379.54))`.] Without the explanation `r pct(one(pa_desc, target == "Human average", explain == "No")$pct_poor)` of the students rated the human average as poor or very poor, against `r pct(one(pa_desc, target == "Human average", explain == "Yes")$pct_poor)` with the explanation. In the adjusted model the explanation raised the odds of a higher rating (odds ratio `r ci(one(pa_eff, target == "Human average", model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)"))`, `r pv(one(pa_eff, target == "Human average", model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)")$p)`), but the unadjusted comparison is weaker (odds ratio `r ci(one(pa_eff, target == "Human average", model == "Ordinal logit, unadjusted (OR)"))`, `r pv(one(pa_eff, target == "Human average", model == "Ordinal logit, unadjusted (OR)")$p)`; Wilcoxon `r pv(one(pa_desc, target == "Human average", explain == "No")$wilcoxon_p)`). This result is borderline and was not corrected for testing two outcomes, so it should be considered exploratory. One reading is that students who had just seen the AI's reasoning were less inclined to dismiss the alternative estimate.

## Experiment 2: Socratic Versus Non-Socratic AI {#sec:res-socratic}

Students then completed three tasks with the help of an AI agent that was randomly Socratic or non-Socratic: a numerical estimate (Task 1), an opinion essay (Task 2) and a physics question on sound (Task 3). Unless stated otherwise, the models are estimated separately for each task, with one observation per student, and adjust for school, the student's self-efficacy for that task and, in Task 3, whether the student answered correctly before using the AI (the pre-specified adjustment set). We report 95% confidence intervals based on HC2 robust errors for linear models and Wald intervals for ordinal-logit models.

### Confidence and learning (RQ3) {#sec:res-rq3}

**Confidence.** Students reported how confident they were that their answer was accurate, on a five-point scale. The distributions are similar in the two groups (Figure \@ref(fig:confidence)). In Tasks 1 and 2 the adjusted difference is essentially zero (Table \@ref(tab:primary)): in Task 1 the Socratic group scored `r num(-c_ols("C1")$est)` points lower on the five-point scale (95% CI `r num(c_ols("C1")$lo)` to `r num(c_ols("C1")$hi)`) and in Task 2 `r num(c_ols("C2")$est)` points higher (`r num(c_ols("C2")$lo)` to `r num(c_ols("C2")$hi)`). In Task 3 the Socratic group was `r num(-c_ols("C3")$est)` points less confident (`r num(c_ols("C3")$lo)` to `r num(c_ols("C3")$hi)`; `r num(-one(conf_size, outcome == "C3")$adj_effect_sd)` standard deviations), which is within the range of chance (`r pv(c_ols("C3")$p)`; randomisation inference `r pv(one(ri, outcome == "C3")$p)`). After the Holm correction across the four primary outcomes the smallest adjusted p-value is `r num(min(holm$p_holm), 2)`. Pooling the three tasks gives a difference of `r ci(conf_pool)` standard deviations (errors clustered by student; `r pv(conf_pool$p)`), and the effect does not differ significantly across tasks (`r pv(conf_pool$p_task_diff)`). The ordinal and linear models agree (Table \@ref(tab:primary)).

```{r primary}
cm <- function(id, a) sprintf("%.2f", conf_desc$mean[conf_desc$task == task_name[[id]] & conf_desc$arm == a])
row_conf <- function(id, lab) {
  o <- c_ols(id)
  r <- one(conf_eff, outcome == id, model == "Ordinal logit, adjusted (OR)")
  tibble(Outcome = lab, `Non-Socratic` = cm(id, "Non-Socratic"), Socratic = cm(id, "Socratic"),
         `Adjusted difference [95% CI]` = ci(o), `Odds ratio [95% CI]` = ci(r),
         p = sprintf("%.2f", o$p), `RI p` = sprintf("%.2f", one(ri, outcome == id)$p), `Holm p` = sprintf("%.2f", one(holm, outcome == id)$p_holm))
}
k_non <- one(corr_desc, arm == "Non-Socratic"); k_soc <- one(corr_desc, arm == "Socratic")
k_row <- one(corr_eff, model == "Adjusted risk difference (LPM, HC2)")
k_or <- corr_or %>% rename(est = or)
rowk <- tibble(Outcome = "Task 3 correct after AI (%)", `Non-Socratic` = sprintf("%.1f", k_non$pct_correct_after),
               Socratic = sprintf("%.1f", k_soc$pct_correct_after),
               `Adjusted difference [95% CI]` = ci(k_row, 100, 1), `Odds ratio [95% CI]` = ci(k_or),
               p = sprintf("%.2f", k_row$p), `RI p` = sprintf("%.2f", one(ri, outcome == "K3")$p), `Holm p` = sprintf("%.2f", one(holm, outcome == "K3")$p_holm))
bind_rows(row_conf("C1", "Confidence, Task 1 (1-5)"), row_conf("C2", "Confidence, Task 2 (1-5)"),
          row_conf("C3", "Confidence, Task 3 (1-5)"), rowk) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", caption = "Primary outcomes: Socratic minus non-Socratic AI. The first two columns are means (confidence) or the percentage correct (Task 3).") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(
    general = paste("Adjusted differences are in scale points for confidence (linear model) and percentage points for correctness (linear probability model);",
                    "odds ratios come from ordinal (confidence) or binary (correctness) logit models. RI p = randomisation-inference p-value (5,000 permutations of the assignment within school);",
                    "Holm p = Holm-adjusted p-value across the four outcomes, based on the adjusted models. N = 120 in every row."),
    general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE
  )
```

```{r confidence, fig.cap = "Students' confidence in their answers by task and AI agent: shares of students at each point of the five-point scale.", out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("confidence_distribution.pdf"))
```

With about `r round(n_an / 2)` students per arm, null results must be read with the precision of the design in mind. The minimum detectable effect (80% power, two-sided 5% test) is about `r num(one(mde, outcome == "C1")$mde, 2)` scale points (`r num(one(mde, outcome == "C1")$mde_sd, 2)` standard deviations) for confidence and `r num(one(mde, outcome == "K3")$mde, 0)` percentage points for correctness. The confidence intervals in Table \@ref(tab:primary) are consistent with true effects of that size in either direction, so we can exclude large effects but not small or moderate ones. The conclusion is robust to the specification (Figure \@ref(fig:forest)): unadjusted models, models with additional covariates (gender, grades, prior AI use and the explanation arm) and fully interacted models give the same signs and similar magnitudes (for instance, in Task 3 the estimates of the effect on confidence range from `r num(min(filter(robust, outcome == "C3", !spec %in% c("Brussels only", "Seville only"))$est))` to `r num(max(filter(robust, outcome == "C3", !spec %in% c("Brussels only", "Seville only"))$est))` points). The Task 3 estimate is larger in Seville (`r num(one(robust, outcome == "C3", spec == "Seville only")$est)` points) than in Brussels (`r num(one(robust, outcome == "C3", spec == "Brussels only")$est)`), but the interaction between school and treatment is not significant for any primary outcome (smallest `r pv(min(het$p))`).

```{r forest, fig.cap = "Adjusted effects of the Socratic AI on the four primary outcomes with 95% confidence intervals. Confidence is expressed in standard deviations of the five-point scale and correctness in percentage points.", out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("summary_forest.pdf"))
```

**Learning.** Task 3 asked whether sound travels faster in water than in air, and why. Before using the AI `r pct(pct_before)` of the students gave the correct answer, and after using it `r pct(pct_after)` did (Figure \@ref(fig:correctness)). The improvement came from students who had been wrong: `r pct(tr_rate("Non-Socratic", 0, 1))` of the initially incorrect students in the non-Socratic group and `r pct(tr_rate("Socratic", 0, 1))` in the Socratic group answered correctly afterwards, while only `r pct(tr_rate("Non-Socratic", 1, 0))` and `r pct(tr_rate("Socratic", 1, 0))` of those initially correct changed to a wrong answer. The two agents were equally effective: the adjusted difference in the probability of a correct final answer is `r num(100 * k_row$est, 1)` percentage points (95% CI `r num(100 * k_row$lo, 1)` to `r num(100 * k_row$hi, 1)`; `r pv(k_row$p)`; odds ratio `r ci(k_or)`). This null result is informative only relative to the minimum detectable effect of about `r num(one(mde, outcome == "K3")$mde, 0)` percentage points. The Socratic group started from a lower baseline (`r pct(corr_desc$pct_correct_before[corr_desc$arm == "Socratic"])` correct against `r pct(corr_desc$pct_correct_before[corr_desc$arm == "Non-Socratic"])`), which is why the models control for the baseline answer.

```{r correctness, fig.cap = "Share of students answering the Task 3 question correctly before and after interacting with the AI agent, by agent type (95% Wilson confidence intervals).", out.width = "65%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("correctness.pdf"))
```

Confidence tracked correctness only weakly. In the non-Socratic group, students whose final answer was right were just `r num(one(calib, arm == "Non-Socratic", post_correct == 1)$mean_confidence - one(calib, arm == "Non-Socratic", post_correct == 0)$mean_confidence)` points more confident than those who were wrong; in the Socratic group the gap was `r num(one(calib, arm == "Socratic", post_correct == 1)$mean_confidence - one(calib, arm == "Socratic", post_correct == 0)$mean_confidence)` points. The gap arises because students who were wrong were less confident with the Socratic agent (`r num(one(calib, arm == "Socratic", post_correct == 0)$mean_confidence)` against `r num(one(calib, arm == "Non-Socratic", post_correct == 0)$mean_confidence)`), but this difference is not significant (`r pv(one(calib_int, term == "z")$p)`), and neither is the interaction between the agent and correctness (`r pv(one(calib_int, term == "z:post_correct")$p)`).

**Retention.** After the tasks, students answered without the AI a related question: in which of five materials (gold, rubber, warm air, cold air, water) does sound travel fastest. Fewer students answered correctly than after the interaction with the AI in Task 3, and the proportion did not differ by agent (Table \@ref(tab:retention)). This result needs a caveat about the data. The stored answers to this question use different codes in the two schools (numeric in Seville, labels borrowed from another scale in Brussels), so which code stands for gold is an inference. Under the coding used in the previous version of this manuscript `r pct(retention$pct_correct[1], 1)` of the students were correct, under an alternative coding that follows the order of the options `r pct(retention$pct_correct[2], 1)`, and using the Seville students alone `r pct(retention$pct_correct[3], 1)`. Under all three codings fewer than half of the students gave the right answer, and the Socratic and non-Socratic groups do not differ (differences between `r num(100 * min(retention$est), 1)` and `r num(100 * max(retention$est), 1)` percentage points; all p-values above `r num(min(retention$p), 2)`). We therefore conclude that many students did not transfer what they had learned with the AI, but we do not report a precise rate until the coding of this item is verified against the original questionnaire.

```{r retention}
retention %>%
  mutate(coding = sub("^[ABC]: ", "", coding), pct = sprintf("%.1f", pct_correct),
         effect = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", num(100 * est, 1), num(100 * lo, 1), num(100 * hi, 1)), p = sprintf("%.2f", p)) %>%
  select(coding, n, pct, effect, p) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "",
                  col.names = c("Coding of the answer 'gold'", "N", "% correct", "Difference, pp [95% CI]", "p"),
                  caption = "Answer to the transfer question (answered without AI) under three codings of the stored responses") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(general = "Difference is Socratic minus non-Socratic (linear probability models with HC2 robust errors, adjusted for school, Task 3 self-efficacy and the baseline answer).",
                       general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE)
```

### Perceived helpfulness (RQ4) {#sec:res-rq4}

Students also rated how helpful it was to interact with the AI tutor. The two schools used different five-point labels (the top category was "Extremely helpful" in Seville and "Very helpful" in Brussels), and the scales were aligned by the position of the labels; we check below that the results do not depend on this choice. Helpfulness is a secondary outcome and is not part of the Holm family.

Students rated the Socratic agent as less helpful in all three tasks, with the clearest difference in Task 1 (Figure \@ref(fig:helpfulness-fig) and Table \@ref(tab:helpfulness)). In Task 1 the adjusted difference is `r num(h_ols("Task 1")$est)` points (95% CI `r num(h_ols("Task 1")$lo)` to `r num(h_ols("Task 1")$hi)`; `r pv(h_ols("Task 1")$p)`), and the share of students who rated the agent as helpful or very helpful is `r num(-100 * one(help_eff, grepl("Task 1", task), grepl("Rated 4-5", model))$est, 0)` percentage points lower (`r pct(one(help_desc, grepl("Task 1", task), arm == "Socratic")$pct_rated_4_5)` against `r pct(one(help_desc, grepl("Task 1", task), arm == "Non-Socratic")$pct_rated_4_5)`). In Task 3 the difference is `r num(h_ols("Task 3")$est)` points (`r num(h_ols("Task 3")$lo)` to `r num(h_ols("Task 3")$hi)`; `r pv(h_ols("Task 3")$p)`), but the ordinal model gives a weaker result (odds ratio `r ci(h_or("Task 3"))`, `r pv(h_or("Task 3")$p)`). In Task 2, the essay, there is no difference (`r num(h_ols("Task 2")$est)` points; `r pv(h_ols("Task 2")$p)`). Pooling the tasks (helpfulness standardised within task, errors clustered by student), the Socratic agent was rated `r num(-help_pool$est)` standard deviations lower (95% CI `r num(-help_pool$hi)` to `r num(-help_pool$lo)`; `r pv(help_pool$p)`), with weak evidence that the size of the difference varies across tasks (`r pv(help_pool$p_task_diff)`). Allowing for three task-level tests, the Holm-adjusted p-values of the linear models are `r paste(sprintf("%.3f", p.adjust(help_eff %>% filter(model == "OLS, adjusted (points)") %>% pull(p), "holm")), collapse = ", ")` for Tasks 1, 2 and 3, so only Task 1 stands as a clear result.

```{r helpfulness}
hrow <- function(k) {
  o <- h_ols(k); r <- h_or(k)
  dn <- one(help_desc, grepl(k, task), arm == "Non-Socratic"); ds <- one(help_desc, grepl(k, task), arm == "Socratic")
  tibble(Task = k,
         `Mean (non-Socratic / Socratic)` = sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", dn$mean, ds$mean),
         `Rated 4-5 (non-Socratic / Socratic)` = sprintf("%.0f%% / %.0f%%", dn$pct_rated_4_5, ds$pct_rated_4_5),
         `Difference, points [95% CI]` = ci(o), `p (linear)` = sprintf("%.3f", o$p),
         `Odds ratio [95% CI]` = ci(r), `p (ordinal)` = sprintf("%.3f", r$p))
}
bind_rows(hrow("Task 1"), hrow("Task 2"), hrow("Task 3")) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", caption = "Perceived helpfulness of the AI agent (1-5): Socratic versus non-Socratic") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(general = "Differences are Socratic minus non-Socratic, adjusted for school and task-specific self-efficacy (and the baseline answer in Task 3); linear models use HC2 robust errors. Odds ratios below 1 mean lower helpfulness ratings with the Socratic agent. N = 120 per task.",
                       general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE)
```

```{r helpfulness-fig, fig.cap = "Perceived helpfulness of the AI agent by task and agent type: shares of students at each point of the five-point scale.", out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("helpfulness_distribution.pdf"))
```

Because the two schools used different labels, we checked that the result does not depend on how the scales are aligned (Table \@ref(tab:helpfulness-checks)). Estimating the Task 1 model separately in each school gives odds ratios of `r num(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 1", task), grepl("Brussels", check))$est)` in Brussels and `r num(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 1", task), grepl("Seville", check))$est)` in Seville, both below 1 although with wide intervals, and recoding Seville's "Very helpful" as the top category (the previous coding) leaves the pooled Task 1 estimate nearly unchanged (odds ratio `r num(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 1", task), grepl("Manuscript", check))$est)`, `r pv(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 1", task), grepl("Manuscript", check))$p)`). In Task 3 the within-school estimates differ (Brussels `r num(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 3", task), grepl("Brussels", check))$est)`, Seville `r num(one(help_chk, grepl("Task 3", task), grepl("Seville", check))$est)`), so the Task 3 result is less secure. In sum, students found the Socratic agent less helpful, most clearly when the task was to estimate a quantity.

```{r helpfulness-checks}
help_chk %>%
  mutate(task = sub(":.*", "", task), check = sub(" \\(ordinal OR\\)", "", check),
         check = sub("Manuscript recode, pooled", "Pooled, alternative recode", check),
         or = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", num(est), num(lo), num(hi)), p = sprintf("%.3f", p)) %>%
  select(task, check, n, or, p) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", col.names = c("Task", "Specification", "N", "Odds ratio [95% CI]", "p"),
                  caption = "Perceived helpfulness: Socratic versus non-Socratic odds ratio under alternative alignments of the two schools' scales") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) %>%
  kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major")
```

### What the Conversations Show (RQ5) {#sec:llm-results}

We now turn to the conversations between students and the AI agents. Two caveats apply to this section. First, the conversation logs identify `r n_accounts` user accounts, fewer than the `r n_all` students in the questionnaire, and `r n_both` of the accounts have conversations in both conditions, so the random intercept in the models below groups conversations by account and may not correspond to a single student.^[This is a data issue that we are still resolving. It does not affect the questionnaire-based results above, which do not use the logs.] Second, the ratings come from LLMs, and agreement between them shows consistency, not validity.

**Interaction volume.** Conversations with the Socratic agent were longer (Table \@ref(tab:volume)). Students sent a median of `r vol$median_socratic[1]` messages per conversation to the Socratic agent and `r vol$median_non_socratic[1]` to the non-Socratic agent (Wilcoxon `r pv(vol$wilcoxon_p[1])`), and wrote a median of `r vol$median_socratic[2]` against `r vol$median_non_socratic[2]` words. In a mixed model that accounts for school, the order of the conversation and the account, Socratic conversations had `r num(vol$ratio[1])` times as many student messages (95% CI `r num(vol$ratio_lo[1])` to `r num(vol$ratio_hi[1])`) and `r num(vol$ratio[2])` times as many student words (`r num(vol$ratio_lo[2])` to `r num(vol$ratio_hi[2])`). The same pattern appears in the number of turns that the Brussels students reported in the questionnaire (medians of `r one(use, grepl("Task 1", task), arm == "Socratic")$median` against `r one(use, grepl("Task 1", task), arm == "Non-Socratic")$median` in Task 1 and `r one(use, grepl("Task 2", task), arm == "Socratic")$median` against `r one(use, grepl("Task 2", task), arm == "Non-Socratic")$median` in Task 2; Wilcoxon tests: `r pv(one(use, grepl("Task 1", task), arm == "Socratic")$wilcoxon_p)` in Task 1, `r pv(one(use, grepl("Task 2", task), arm == "Socratic")$wilcoxon_p)` in Task 2 and `r pv(one(use, grepl("Task 3", task), arm == "Socratic")$wilcoxon_p)` in Task 3). Because the Socratic agent was instructed to reply with questions, this difference follows in part from the condition itself, and it is not evidence that students were more engaged or thought harder.

```{r volume}
vol %>%
  transmute(Measure = measure, `Median, non-Socratic` = median_non_socratic, `Median, Socratic` = median_socratic,
            `Wilcoxon p` = ifelse(wilcoxon_p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", wilcoxon_p)),
            `Ratio Socratic / non-Socratic [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", ratio, ratio_lo, ratio_hi),
            `Mixed-model p` = ifelse(p_mixed < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_mixed))) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = "lccccc", caption = "Student messages and words per conversation, by agent (all 354 conversations)") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "2.6cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2:3, width = "2.2cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(4, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(5, width = "3.2cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(6, width = "1.8cm") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(general = "Ratios are from linear mixed models of the logarithm of each count with a random intercept for the account and fixed effects for school and conversation order.",
                       general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE)
```

**Agreement between the raters.** We analyse the 314 holdout conversations (`r llm$students[1]` accounts; `r vol_desc$chats[vol_desc$arm == "non_socratic"]` with the non-Socratic and `r vol_desc$chats[vol_desc$arm == "socratic"]` with the Socratic agent), and report the agreement of the two raters in Table \@ref(tab:reliability). Among the student-behaviour items, reasoning quality (Krippendorff's alpha `r num(one(rel, mode == "full", item == "reasoning_quality")$alpha)`) and knowledge building (`r num(one(rel, mode == "full", item == "knowledge_building")$alpha)`) reached the pre-specified threshold of 0.67 and are our primary outcomes. Effort and task focus fell just short (`r num(one(rel, mode == "full", item == "effort_seriousness")$alpha, 3)`), and the yes/no question item reached `r pct(one(rel, mode == "full", item == "question_asking")$pct_agree)` agreement against the threshold of 80%. We report these two as exploratory. None of the four items describing the AI agent's Socratic conduct reached the threshold (alpha between `r num(min(rel_c$alpha))` and `r num(max(rel_c$alpha))`). The two raters differed in leniency but ranked the conversations similarly (rank correlations of `r num(min(rel_c$spearman))` to `r num(max(rel_c$spearman))` for these items), so the results on the agent's conduct are exploratory.

```{r reliability}
labs <- c(reasoning_quality = "Reasoning quality", knowledge_building = "Knowledge building", effort_seriousness = "Effort and task focus",
          question_asking = "Asks a content question", supportive_guidance = "Supportive guidance", next_step_guidance = "Next-step guidance",
          encouraging_tone = "Encouraging tone", conversational_flow = "Conversational flow")
rel %>%
  filter(mode == "full", item %in% names(labs)) %>%
  mutate(Group = ifelse(rubric == "student", "Student behaviour", "AI agent conduct"), Item = labs[item],
         Agreement = ifelse(is.na(pct_agree), sprintf("alpha = %.2f", alpha), sprintf("%.0f%% agreement, AC1 = %.2f", pct_agree, ac1)),
         Spearman = sprintf("%.2f", spearman), Status = ifelse(status == "primary", "Primary", "Exploratory")) %>%
  arrange(desc(rubric == "student"), match(item, names(labs))) %>%
  select(Group, Item, Agreement, Spearman, Status) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", caption = "Agreement between the two LLM raters on the 314 holdout conversations") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) %>%
  kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major")
```

**AI agent conduct.** The Socratic agent was rated clearly higher on supportive guidance without giving the answer (`r ci(one(llm, item == "supportive_guidance", spec == "adjusted"))` standardised units), next-step guidance (`r ci(one(llm, item == "next_step_guidance", spec == "adjusted"))`) and encouraging tone (`r ci(one(llm, item == "encouraging_tone", spec == "adjusted"))`), and both raters agreed on the direction and approximate size of these differences (Table \@ref(tab:si-per-rater) in the Supporting Information). Conversational flow was higher after adjusting for message counts (`r ci(one(llm, item == "conversational_flow", spec == "adjusted"))`) but not before (`r ci(one(llm, item == "conversational_flow", spec == "unadjusted"))`), so we do not interpret it. Although the reliability of these items is below our threshold, the large and consistent differences support the view that the two agents behaved as instructed.

**Observable student behaviour.** Table \@ref(tab:llm-effects) and Figure \@ref(fig:llm-effects-fig) compare the students' conversations. Without adjustment, students with the Socratic agent scored higher on reasoning quality (`r ci(one(llm, item == "reasoning_quality", spec == "unadjusted"))`), knowledge building (`r ci(one(llm, item == "knowledge_building", spec == "unadjusted"))`) and effort (`r ci(one(llm, item == "effort_seriousness", spec == "unadjusted"))`). Most of this difference is mechanical: the number and length of the student's messages alone account for about half of the variation in these scores (marginal R-squared between `r num(min(filter(llm_r2, item %in% c("reasoning_quality", "knowledge_building", "effort_seriousness"))$R2_length_only))` and `r num(max(filter(llm_r2, item %in% c("reasoning_quality", "knowledge_building", "effort_seriousness"))$R2_length_only))`), and the Socratic agent prompts more and longer messages.

After adjusting for the number of student messages and words, the difference remained for reasoning quality (`r ci(one(llm, item == "reasoning_quality", spec == "adjusted"))`; Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted `r pv(one(llm, item == "reasoning_quality", spec == "adjusted")$p_bh)`) and was smaller and borderline for knowledge building (`r ci(one(llm, item == "knowledge_building", spec == "adjusted"))`; adjusted `r pv(one(llm, item == "knowledge_building", spec == "adjusted")$p_bh)`). The exploratory items point the same way: effort (`r ci(one(llm, item == "effort_seriousness", spec == "adjusted"))`) and asking a content question (`r ci(one(llm, item == "question_asking", spec == "adjusted"))` on the 0-1 scale; `r pv(one(llm, item == "question_asking", spec == "adjusted")$p)`).

The reasoning result was stable across the pre-specified checks (Table \@ref(tab:si-sensitivity) in the Supporting Information): it was similar when the rater saw only the student's messages (`r ci(one(llm_sens, analysis == "student-only ratings", item == "reasoning_quality"))`), when conversations with a single student message were excluded (`r ci(one(llm_sens, analysis == "excl. 1-message chats", item == "reasoning_quality"))`), when the development conversations were added (`r ci(one(llm_sens, analysis == "all chats (holdout + development)", item == "reasoning_quality"))`), and for each rater analysed alone (`r num(one(llm_rater, item == "reasoning_quality", model == "claude-haiku-5-5")$est)` and `r num(one(llm_rater, item == "reasoning_quality", model == "gpt-4o-mini")$est)`). The knowledge-building result was less robust: it was close to zero for the Claude rater alone (`r ci(one(llm_rater, item == "knowledge_building", model == "claude-haiku-5-5"))`) and positive for the GPT rater (`r ci(one(llm_rater, item == "knowledge_building", model == "gpt-4o-mini"))`). We therefore regard the evidence for more observable reasoning with the Socratic agent as moderate, and the evidence for knowledge building as weak. These are ratings of what is visible in the transcript, not measures of learning; and, as shown above, the Socratic condition did not improve the Task 3 answers.

```{r llm-effects}
llm %>%
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", est, lo, hi)) %>%
  select(family, item, status, spec, cell, p_bh) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = spec, values_from = c(cell, p_bh)) %>%
  arrange(family, match(item, names(labs))) %>%
  mutate(Group = ifelse(grepl("^A", family), "Student behaviour", "AI agent conduct"), Item = labs[item],
         Status = ifelse(status == "primary", "Primary", "Exploratory"),
         p_adj = ifelse(p_bh_adjusted < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_bh_adjusted))) %>%
  select(Group, Item, Status, cell_unadjusted, cell_adjusted, p_adj) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", col.names = c("Group", "Item", "Status", "Unadjusted [95% CI]", "Adjusted [95% CI]", "BH p (adjusted)"),
                  caption = "Socratic minus non-Socratic differences in LLM-coded conversations (314 holdout conversations). Scores are standardised averages of two LLM raters (the yes/no item is a proportion).") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "scale_down") %>%
  kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major") %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(general = "Linear mixed models with a random intercept for the account and fixed effects for school and conversation order. Adjusted models also control for the logarithm of the number of student messages and words. BH = Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value within the four items of each group.",
                       general_title = "Notes: ", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = TRUE)
```

```{r llm-effects-fig, fig.cap = "Socratic minus non-Socratic differences in LLM-coded conversations, unadjusted and adjusted for message and word counts (95% confidence intervals).", out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("fig_llm_effects.pdf"))
```

## Exploratory Analyses {#sec:res-exploratory}

**Heterogeneity by school.** For none of the four primary outcomes does the effect of the Socratic agent differ between Brussels and Seville (interaction p-values between `r num(min(het$p), 2)` and `r num(max(het$p), 2)`). The questionnaire pipeline does not include the other planned subgroup analyses (prior ChatGPT experience, gender and task), and the sample is too small to support them reliably.

**Changing opinions in the essay task.** Task 2 had no correct answer, so we cannot measure accuracy, but we can ask whether the agent moved students' opinions about the effect of social media on teenagers. More students with the Socratic agent changed their opinion after the interaction (`r pct(op_desc$pct_changed[op_desc$arm == "Socratic"])` against `r pct(op_desc$pct_changed[op_desc$arm == "Non-Socratic"])`; adjusted difference `r num(100 * one(op_eff, grepl("Changed", outcome))$est, 1)` percentage points, 95% CI `r num(100 * one(op_eff, grepl("Changed", outcome))$lo, 1)` to `r num(100 * one(op_eff, grepl("Changed", outcome))$hi, 1)`, `r pv(one(op_eff, grepl("Changed", outcome))$p)`), and the average size of the change was larger (`r ci(one(op_eff, grepl("Absolute", outcome)))` points, `r pv(one(op_eff, grepl("Absolute", outcome))$p)`). The signed shift does not differ significantly (`r ci(one(op_eff, grepl("Signed", outcome)))`, `r pv(one(op_eff, grepl("Signed", outcome))$p)`), which suggests that the Socratic agent moved opinions in both directions and not in one. These tests were not corrected for multiplicity and are exploratory.
